title: The Formation of the Solar System
subject: astro
paras: For centuries, scientists have tried to explain why the planets of the solar system share certain regular features. All eight planets orbit the Sun in the same direction, and their orbits lie roughly in a single flat plane. The Sun itself rotates in that same direction. In the eighteenth century, the philosopher Immanuel Kant and the mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace independently proposed that these patterns were not accidental: they were clues that the Sun and planets had formed together from a single rotating cloud of gas and dust. This idea, known as the nebular hypothesis, remains the foundation of modern theories of planetary formation.

According to the current version of the theory, about 4.6 billion years ago a cloud of cold gas and dust in our galaxy began to collapse under its own gravity, perhaps triggered by the shock wave of a nearby exploding star. As the cloud contracted, it began to spin faster, in the same way that a figure skater spins faster when she pulls in her arms. The spinning also caused the cloud to flatten into a disk. Most of the material fell toward the center, where pressure and temperature rose until nuclear fusion began and the Sun was born. The remaining material, perhaps one or two percent of the total, stayed in the surrounding disk, which astronomers call a protoplanetary disk.

Within this disk, tiny grains of dust collided and stuck together, gradually forming larger clumps. Over thousands of years, these clumps grew into bodies a few kilometers across, called planetesimals. [■] Once planetesimals became large enough, their gravity began to pull in additional material, and growth accelerated. [■] The largest bodies swept up smaller ones in their paths, becoming protoplanets the size of the Moon or Mars. [■] Collisions between these protoplanets were common and often violent. [■]

Temperature played a key role in deciding what kind of planet formed where. Close to the young Sun, the disk was so hot that only materials with high melting points, such as metals and rocky minerals, could remain solid. The planets that formed there, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are therefore small and composed mainly of rock and metal. Farther out, beyond a boundary known as the frost line, it was cold enough for water, ammonia, and methane to freeze into ice. Because ice was far more abundant than rock, planetary cores in this region could grow much larger. Some became massive enough to capture enormous amounts of hydrogen and helium gas directly from the disk, producing the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn.

The nebular hypothesis received strong support near the end of the twentieth century, when telescopes began to observe young stars surrounded by flattened disks of dust. Some of these disks contain dark rings and gaps, which many astronomers interpret as paths cleared by planets in the process of forming. Since 1995, astronomers have also discovered thousands of planets orbiting other stars, confirming that planet formation is a common outcome of star formation.

These discoveries, however, have also complicated the picture. Many distant systems contain giant planets orbiting extremely close to their stars, where, according to the basic theory, such planets could not have formed. To explain them, astronomers have proposed that planets can migrate, moving inward or outward after formation through gravitational interactions with the disk or with other planets. Some researchers now suggest that Jupiter itself may have moved inward and then back outward early in the solar system's history, a journey that could explain why Mars is so small. The basic outline of the nebular hypothesis remains widely accepted, but the details of how planets reach their final positions are still actively debated.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, which of the following observations led Kant and Laplace to propose the nebular hypothesis?
opts: The planets differ greatly in size.
The planets orbit in the same direction in nearly the same plane.
The Sun is much larger than any planet.
Some planets have moons.
qs.why: 第1段：All eight planets orbit the Sun in the same direction… a single flat plane… these patterns were… clues。

qs.q: The word "independently" in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
opts: separately
reluctantly
publicly
correctly
qs.why: independently proposed 指两人各自独立提出。

qs.q: Why does the author mention "a figure skater" in paragraph 2?
opts: To compare the speed of the collapsing cloud with human motion
To illustrate why a contracting cloud spins faster
To suggest that the Sun formed from a moving object
To explain why the disk became hot
qs.why: 类比说明云收缩时转速加快。

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, what happened to most of the material in the collapsing cloud?
opts: It formed the planets.
It escaped into space.
It fell toward the center and formed the Sun.
It froze into ice beyond the frost line.
qs.why: Most of the material fell toward the center… and the Sun was born。只有1–2%留在盘中。

qs.q: Look at the four squares [■] that indicate where the following sentence could be added to paragraph 3. "In this way, a few dominant bodies came to control each region of the disk." Where would the sentence best fit?
opts: After the first square
After the second square
After the third square
After the fourth square
qs.why: In this way 承接上一句“大天体扫掉小天体”，接着才讲原行星之间的碰撞。

qs.q: According to paragraph 4, why were planets beyond the frost line able to grow much larger?
opts: They were closer to the Sun.
Ice was much more plentiful than rock there.
Metals were more common there.
They formed earlier than the inner planets.
qs.why: Because ice was far more abundant than rock, planetary cores in this region could grow much larger。

qs.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars?
opts: They formed in a region where ice could not remain solid.
They captured large amounts of hydrogen gas.
They formed beyond the frost line.
They contain more ice than Jupiter.
qs.why: 它们靠近太阳，那里太热，只有金属和岩石能保持固态。

qs.q: The word "them" in paragraph 6 ("To explain them") refers to
opts: distant systems
giant planets orbiting extremely close to their stars
astronomers
gravitational interactions
qs.why: them 指上句中离恒星极近的巨行星。

qs.q: According to paragraphs 5 and 6, all of the following support or refine the nebular hypothesis EXCEPT
opts: observations of dusty disks around young stars
gaps in disks that may be cleared by forming planets
the discovery of thousands of planets around other stars
evidence that the Sun formed after the planets
qs.why: 文中说太阳先在中心形成，没有“太阳晚于行星”的证据。

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: The nebular hypothesis explains how the solar system formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust.
opts: A collapsing, spinning cloud flattened into a disk, with most material forming the Sun at the center.
Dust grains in the disk gradually grew into planetesimals and then protoplanets.
Kant was a philosopher and Laplace was a mathematician.
Differences in temperature across the disk explain why rocky planets formed near the Sun and giant planets farther out.
Mars is the smallest planet in the solar system.
The shock wave of an exploding star definitely caused the collapse.
qs.why: C 是细节；E 与原文不符（原文只说火星小）；F 原文用 perhaps，不确定。
